newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela comes in from cold with big share issue.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela comes in from cold with big share issue.

text.p: Venezuela, so long the economic outcast in Latin America, basked in the spotlight Friday as shares in national telephone company CANTV debuted on local and international markets with an impressive flourish.

The $1.1 billion global issue of CANTV -- one of the largest to come out of Latin America in recent years -- was billed as the first serious test of the reform program started by President Rafael Caldera's government seven months ago.

"What happened today ratifies the Venezuelan government's commitment to press ahead with the process of modernizing its economy," Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar told a news conference in New York.

The issue, which was priced at $23 per American Depository Receipt (ADR), led trading volume on the New York Stock Exchange. The ADRs closed up over 12 percent at $25-7/8. Underwriters said the issue was oversubscribed three times.
"What we saw in the market was confidence in the country and this will give a push to the other privatizations," Matos said.
Caldera, 80, abandoned two years of protectionist policies in April and launched a program which quickly received backing from the International Monetary Fund.

Recently buoyed by a flood of revenues from higher-than- expected oil prices Venezuela has ridden a tide of optimism, but analysts have grown increasingly concerned that Caldera's commitment to more lasting reforms was weak.
"The CANTV sale has provided a very positive psychological push to the reforms," said Caracas-based consultant Frank Amador.

Officials have touted the Compania Anonima Nacional Telefonos de Venezuela issue as the start of popular capitalism in Venezuela, a country where many businesses are still family-owned and the stock market is open for just over four hours a day.
About 0.5 percent of the population received shares in the issue -- a small, but important start, officials said.
On the excited floor of the Caracas Stock Exchange, exchange President Alejandro Salcedo said, "It's a great event that 83,000 Venezuelans have been brought together in this process."
One local businessman recounted how even office messengers had asked for advances on Christmas bonuses to buy shares which were offered on favorable credit terms.

But for most Venezuelans -- 80 percent of whom live in poverty -- the daily struggle of survival and coping with an inflation rate running at more than 100 percent mean the mysteries of the stock market remain distant.
"They say it's good news but not if you cannot afford to buy the shares," said taxi driver Jorge Morrales.
